pr_title: Set `attributes_for_inspect` to `[:id]` in the production environment only
pr_body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/52728

This Pull Request has been created because we received feedback on a few things about the `attributes_for_inspect` feature introduced in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/49765, specifically around the default settings for this feature, which is `[:id]` in production and `:all` in test and dev. The issues are:

1. This feature should be opt in, and be `:all` in production for upgrading apps.
2. We should always use `:all` in the production console to not hinder debugging/
3. We should not use `consider_all_requests_local` to determine what to set it to

### Detail

To address 1 and 3, I changed how the defaults are set. Now the default value is `:all`, and I set it to `[:id]` in `production.rb`. This means it is also opt in as upgrading apps will need to add that line to their `production.rb`.

For 2, I used the `console` method in the active record railtie to set this it to `:all` in production in the console

### Additional information

<!-- Provide additional information such as benchmarks, references to other repositories, or alternative solutions. -->

### Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

* [x] This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
* [x] Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: `[Fix #issue-number]`
* [x] Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
* [ ] CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.

Why not use `new_defaults` to make the default `[:id]` for new apps and upgrading apps? Since it's faster.

@zzak What is `new_defaults`, sorry I am not familiar with that and I am not seeing it in the code base. Do you just mean a framework default or something different? But I think in general it's a problem since `[:id]` is just the default wanted for prod but `:all` for dev and test - I don't think we can check the env at the time the default is applied.

issue_context.title: Only `id` is shown  when inspecting records in Rails console in production
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce
1. Create a new Rails app (with either Rails 7.2.1 or 8.0.0.alpha): `rails new test-app`
2. Modify `config/database.yml` so that the production database points to the development database (it's fine to keep sqlite for this demonstration):
   ```yml
   default: &default
   adapter: sqlite3
   pool: <%= ENV.fetch("RAILS_MAX_THREADS") { 5 } %>
   timeout: 5000

   development:
     <<: *default
     database: storage/development.sqlite3
   production:
     <<: *default
     database: storage/development.sqlite3
  
3. Create a dummy model: `bin/rails g model User name surname`

Now, if you enter the dev console with `bin/rails c` this is what you'll see:
```rb
test-app(dev)> User.create(name: "John", surname: "Doe")
test-app(dev)> User.first
=> #<User:0x0000000120d516c0 id: 1, name: "John", surname: "Doe", created_at: "2024-08-28 07:12:10.878368000 +0000", updated_at: "2024-08-28 07:12:10.878368000 +0000">
```

And if you enter the console in production with `bin/rails c -e production`, you'll see this:
```rb
test-ap(prod)> User.first
=> #<User:0x000000011f7f8760 id: 1>
```

As you see, while inspecting the user I only get back the `id`.

Note that if you follow those steps with Rails 7.1, the output of the development and production console match (they both show all the attributes).

### Expected behavior
<!-- Tell us what should happen -->
I expect to see all the object attributes even on production. This behavior has changed from Rails 7.2.

### Actual behavior
<!-- Tell us what happens instead -->
From Rails 7.2 onwards, when inspecting a model instance in the production console you only get back the id and not the whole set of attributes.

### System configuration
**Rails version**:
7.2.1

**Ruby version**:
3.3.4
comments: This is expected, set `config.active_record.attributes_for_inspect = :all` for previous behaviour. See #49765

@Earlopain Thanks for you response!

It definitely makes sense to allow this to be configured by the user, however I have a few doubts about the fact that `config.active_record.attributes_for_inspect = :all` is not the default in all environments 🤔.

The PR motivation is:
> This Pull Request has been created because we noticed that ActiveRecord::Core#inspect was taking >9s to run for some large objects in production. This is because the parameter filter is be executed for every attribute.

I am thinking about how many Rails app have such large objects? 
In my opinion, it would have made more sense to default to `config.active_record.attributes_for_inspect = :all` everywhere and only user facing very slow load time for big objects should have to tweak this config.

I mean, most Rails apps probably aren't ever gonna have those types of slow load issues, the risk is that the line `config.active_record.attributes_for_inspect = :all` will be present in every `config/environments/production.rb` of almost all small-medium size Rails apps 🤔.

Maybe I should open a discussion for it?

I don't think you need 9s for a single object for this to make sense. 9s is up there for sure but I myself ran into this multiple times when I've got a larger collection of individual records with few attributes. It does depend on your environment (_not_ the RAILS_ENV kind) if this is even a problem for you (latency, speed, etc.).

I can see how this can be confusing and wonder if something like the hint about calling `connection` when printing the model can be implemented in somewhere. I didn't test this but you should be able to call `full_inspect` regardless of what the config value holds.

@Earlopain I see your point. 
I guess I can close this since this is definitely expected behaviour 👍🏻.

My whole team is also on the `:all` should be default. The current default is next to useless. For many apps, there isn't actually a standard array of field names that you could set across all objects for inspect. I'm actually going to be fairly surprised if most Rails users are happy with this change. We immediately set this to all locally. This is the worst change I've seen to Rails in the 12 years I've been using Rails.
Just to confirm, you all are finding difference when running `rails console` in production right? Not calling `to_s` in logs?
I was actually also seeing this change in development as well. It wasn't just in production.

Hi @jmkoni sorry that this feature is causing you trouble! I just checked on a fresh Rails app, and this feature is not enabled in development mode, as expected. Can you share steps to reproduce how you were seeing this in development mode?

> For many apps, there isn't actually a standard array of field names that you could set across all objects for inspect.

Just a note about this, this setting is configurable per model so you can assign different attributes for inspect for different models.

@jmkoni The way we check this in dev and test is by using the `consider_all_requests_local` setting, which is `true` in dev and test by default. So if you are setting that to `false` in development you would see different behaviour
We ran into the same issue. This default option doesn't make sense at all since it renders the console pretty much unusable.

> The way we check this in dev and test is by using the consider_all_requests_local setting

That doesn't sound reasonable to me... feels more like an end-run around the prohibition on directly checking `Rails.env`. Apart from being a proxy for a particular set of environments, I don't see a connection between request-locality and desired inspection result.

review_comments:
If we do `Model.allocate.inspect` with `attributes_for_inspect = :all` we will get a no method error since `@attributes` is `nil`. So I introduced this method. We can't do `self.class.attribute_names` since it will not include virtual columns.

Alternatively we could update active model to be resilient to `@attributes` being `nil`, but there are already `nil` checks for `@attributes` in this code so I thought it was okay to continue that practice. But I am open to feedback.

We already do this check on line 812. 
Maybe `inspect_with_attributes` should not accept `attributes_to_list` but just call `attributes_for_inspect` itself?
Yeah that's what I would do, however, we also need to pass this from `full_inspect` which also calls `inspect_with_attributes`.

Maybe:
```ruby
    def inspect_with_attributes(attributes_for_inspect=self.class.attributes_for_inspect)
      inspection = if @attributes
        attributes_to_list = if attributes_for_inspect == :all
          all_attributes_for_inspect
        else
          self.class.attributes_for_inspect
        end
        attributes_to_list.filter_map do |name|
          name = name.to_s
          if _has_attribute?(name)
            "#{name}: #{attribute_for_inspect(name)}"
          end
        end.join(", ")
      else
        "not initialized"
      end
      "#<#{self.class} #{inspection}>"
    end

    def full_inspect
      inspect_with_attributes(:all)
    end
```

The problem is that we can't call `self.class.attributes_for_inspect` because it won't include virtual columns (there is a test testing for this).

I did think about going in something like this direction but I am not sure if it's any less complicated 🤔
I guess we could call `self.class.attributes_for_inspect` as the default param and then `self.attributes_for_inspect` in the method body but it's somewhat awkward.

~~If the default is already `:all` above, why do we need to set this here?~~

Edit: ahh, I see because we change the default to `[:id]` in production.rb below for new apps.
